extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, stakeholders, advocates, and community groups who want to submit effective public comments to local, state, or federal decision-makers (including NEPA commenters and historic preservation advocates)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for writing and delivering effective, substantive public comments on regulatory actions, environmental reviews, hearings, and preservation matters across local, state, and federal processes. Emphasizes legal/regulatory anchors (e.g., NEPA), clarity, evidence, scope, and respectful engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and understand the regulatory document
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and understand the regulatory document you are commenting on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by understanding the notice, proposed rule, EIS/EA, or other decision document. If you don’t understand something, use the agency contact to ask clarifying questions before submitting comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor comments to the agency's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor your comment to the agency’s role; align comments with the responsibilities of the agency or decision-maker you’re addressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different bodies review different aspects of a project—county boards, federal agencies, and state offices have distinct authorities. Address the decision-maker’s jurisdiction and avoid irrelevant points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet deadlines and note time zone specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Take careful note of when comment periods end: date, time, and time zone are important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin preparing well before the deadline and confirm whether times are Standard or Daylight Time. Missing the precise deadline can nullify your comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask agency contacts for clarification but submit formally
rubrics_metrics.description: Feel free to reach out to the agency with questions about the document’s meaning; submit official comments through the proper process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency contacts can clarify intent or meaning but cannot substitute for submitting a formal comment via the required form, email, or hearing process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly identify issues and cite specific locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly identify the issues within the regulatory action on which you are commenting and, if commenting on specific text, provide page/column/paragraph citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pinpoint the exact wording or analysis you challenge to make it easier for reviewers to find and respond to your point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select issues strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rule raises many issues, select those you understand best or that affect you most; you do not need to comment on every proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing on fewer, well-supported issues is more effective than addressing everything superficially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to agency-posed questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies often ask specific questions in proposals; answers that directly address these are especially useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep responses on-topic and aligned to the agency’s explicit requests to increase the chance they will be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be constructive and information-rich
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive, information-rich comment that supports its claims is more likely to influence decision-making than vague opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide data, citations, examples, or suggested solutions rather than only emotional or unsupported statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid subjective, vague, or non-specific comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-specific comments that read as a 'vote' (e.g., 'I do not support this project at all') are not considered substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEPA and many agencies require concrete rationale, data, or identification of deficiencies in analysis to treat comments as substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep comments professional and respectful
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep your comment professional; avoid sarcasm or personal attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Politeness builds credibility; attacking people undermines your argument and reduces influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be succinct and precise
rubrics_metrics.description: Be succinct—shape your comment with only the words needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precision respects reviewers’ time and makes your point clearer. Time-limited hearings especially require brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest alternatives and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: If you disagree, suggest an alternative (including no regulation) and explain how the alternative meets objectives or is more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing feasible alternatives makes your objection actionable and increases likelihood of meaningful consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain reasoning and anticipate counterpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequately explain the reasoning behind your position and address likely counterpoints in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong objections anticipate agency rationales and show why they are incomplete or flawed, reducing agency discretion to dismiss the comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify credentials and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify professional or personal experience that distinguishes your comment (scientist, attorney, archaeologist, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider submitting separate professional and personal comments to provide both perspectives and clearly state capacity (personal vs representative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish personal opinions from professional statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly distinguish when you speak personally and when you speak in a professional capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example phrasing: 'I submit this comment in a personal capacity' or 'As a [profession], I offer the following.' This helps agencies weigh expertise appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor NEPA objections in statutory/regulatory duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame NEPA objections as failures to meet statutory/regulatory duties (procedural violations, analytical gaps, public participation deficiencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin NEPA-based claims with explicit references to statutes or CEQ regulations and cite the specific sections to make them legally cognizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite primary sources and the administrative record
rubrics_metrics.description: Support comments with primary sources—EIS appendices, hydrology models, archaeological inventories, engineering drawings, or peer-reviewed studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show what the record omits and use contrastive evidence; agencies are more likely to respond to verifiable, sourced critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate analytical gaps and missing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenge omissions such as missing visual simulations, outdated models, or failure to analyze reasonable alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 40 C.F.R. § 1502.14 and related rules, agencies must analyze a reasonable range of alternatives and cumulative impacts; point to specific regulatory requirements when they are unmet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide quantitative and qualitative economic impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments on economic effects that include quantitative and qualitative data are especially helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give figures, references, or data-backed arguments on costs, funding sources, ROI, or economic trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include personal impact narratives when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use first-person examples to show how the proposed action would impact you personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal stories help reviewers grasp real-world consequences, but should be factual and tied to the decision’s scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pros/cons and discuss trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the pros and cons and trade-offs of your position and respond to other points of view with facts and reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledging trade-offs and proposing mitigations demonstrates balanced, constructive engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-check and verify details
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-check your submissions—verify historical and technical details before asserting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors reduce credibility; always verify newspaper claims, historical dates, or technical assertions before including them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread and be wary of automated drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Always proofread your submission; if you use tools like ChatGPT, proofread the output before submitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clean, typo-free comment appears more thoughtful and avoids introducing errors from automated drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogies sparingly to clarify complex impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: If helpful, use analogies to illustrate interconnected impacts (e.g., incremental changes forcing larger infrastructure needs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies can make technical trade-offs understandable but should not replace evidence or precise analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred file formats and attachments handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid specialized file formats (.docx, .pages); use PDF and upload attachments rather than embedding images in online editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt standardized attachment names (Attachment1_<title>) and be mindful of agency upload limits (e.g., file counts and total MB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep copies and confirm submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a copy of your comment saved in multiple places and wait for a confirmation message before navigating away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saved copies help if web forms fail and are useful for reading at hearings or follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarize yourself with meeting procedures (Robert’s Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarize yourself with Robert’s Rules of Order or applicable parliamentary procedure for meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding meeting rules helps you participate effectively and avoid procedural missteps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing logistics: time limits and required information
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of hearing time limits (commonly 3 minutes) and that you may need to provide full name and mailing address on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice to fit within time limits; if representing an organization, state that at the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pooling time and sign-up rules for hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers can sometimes pool time with others, subject to venue rules and presence requirements for donated time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check sign-up deadlines (often the day before) and ensure donors of time are present or the donation may be invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of presentations at hearings/open houses
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, you may be able to submit or use a PowerPoint—verify availability and coordinate with organizers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a shared presentation with multiple speakers, plan transitions; many venues may not support multimedia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open house participation tips
rubrics_metrics.description: When attending open houses, review posters and looped presentations and allow 30–60 minutes to digest materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open houses are usually self-guided; ask questions of agency staff and confirm whether written comments can be submitted after the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-submission posting and reasons for withholding
rubrics_metrics.description: After submission, comments may be posted publicly; agencies may withhold comments for reasons such as duplicates, PII, profanity, or spam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include sensitive PII if you want the comment posted; agencies may also withhold proprietary or culturally sensitive location data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form letters and mass-submission limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Form letters and mass submissions can help show public sentiment but often carry less weight than unique, substantive comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bundled filings; submit individually if you want each to count separately. Co-signed letters are typically counted once unless agency says otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous comments and standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Some processes accept anonymous comments, but anonymous submissions often do not provide standing for later administrative or judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide contact information if you need legal standing for future appeals; note that anything submitted becomes public record unless the submitter requests otherwise and agency grants confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific written comment criteria under 36 CFR 218.2
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific written comments must be within the scope of the proposed action, directly relate to it, and include supporting reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific comments help responsible officials consider objections; weak objections are easily dismissed while strong ones point to record inconsistencies or legal/analytical flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish substantive vs. non-substantive comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments are substantive if they question adequacy/accuracy, cause changes in alternatives, or provide new relevant information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive comments usually include citations, data, or analysis that identify defects or omissions in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay in scope and stay focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and courts consider only issues within the scope of the decision; stay focused on what the decision-maker can lawfully act on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drifting into unrelated grievances, historical disputes unrelated to the action, or broad policy objections that the agency cannot resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA-specific response strategy phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: When raising NEPA objections, begin claims with: 'This comment identifies a deficiency under [specific section] of NEPA/CEQ regulations…'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit phrasing helps agency staff recognize legally cognizable objections and links the comment to regulatory duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrastive evidence to show omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use contrastive evidence to show what the record omits (e.g., missing visual simulations or underestimated cumulative impacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to specific missing analyses, data, or precedent and explain their relevance to the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose feasible mitigation and alternatives under NEPA
rubrics_metrics.description: Under NEPA, propose feasible alternatives and mitigation measures the agency failed to analyze.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 40 C.F.R. § 1502.14 and demonstrate why the proposed alternatives are reasonable and should have been considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historic-preservation: favor alternative compliance over demolition
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative compliance allows historic buildings to meet the intent of modern codes via compensatory measures instead of forcing full modern retrofits or demolition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask that agencies evaluate performance-based solutions (partial sprinklers, alarms, compartmentalization, phased remediation) and require documented analysis if demolition is claimed necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question formal determinations and request documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a building is labeled 'unsafe,' ask whether a formal order was issued, under which code authority, and what remediation pathways were required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request written orders, dates, code citations, hazards identified, and evaluations of alternative compliance before accepting demolition as the only option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who to engage: stakeholder outreach checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage a broad set of stakeholders (residents, city/county/state agencies, SHPO, federal agencies, tribal nations, preservation professionals, nonprofits, business organizations, media, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early, wide engagement prevents blind spots, protects procedural integrity, and builds credibility; use appropriate partners for research, technical analysis, and civic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider comprehensive topic checklist when unsure what to say
rubrics_metrics.description: If unsure, evaluate the proposal across categories: environmental impacts, community impacts, health & safety, infrastructure, development purpose, regulatory compliance, sustainability/innovation, cost/funding, aesthetics/design, public engagement, and operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the checklist sub-items (e.g., water quality, wildlife, air quality, local economy, noise, occupational hazards, transportation, utilities, permitting, renewable resources, budget, architecture, transparency, maintenance) as prompts for specific, evidence-based comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay involved after submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the final documents and meeting minutes to see how the agency addressed concerns and stay engaged across multiple comment periods or hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may group similar suggestions; continued monitoring lets you follow up, appeal, or participate in later phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor collaboration and creative solutions over simple compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek collaborative solutions that maximize shared values rather than half-measures that leave all parties unsatisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose win-win options that respect preservation and development goals, illustrating mutual benefits (e.g., adaptive reuse instead of demolition).
